claim: Women in Japan and South Korea have achieved the first and fourth highest life expectancy in the world.
source: These gains may partially account for the fact that women in Japan and South Korea have achieved the first and fourth highest life expectancy in the world (see also below).
evidence: This is a statement of fact about life expectancy.

claim: Prior studies have documented a rise in stunting in children in sub-Saharan Africa which continued to the mid-1990s.
source: Prior studies have documented a rise in stunting in children in sub-Saharan Africa which continued to the mid-1990s (Stevens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research findings.

claim: Childhood adversity in sub-Saharan Africa may have carried forward to adulthood and be affecting health in the region.
source: Our results indicate that such childhood adversity may have carried forward to adulthood and be affecting health in the region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to prior research.

claim: The early African advantage over Asia in height may have been partly due to having a more diverse diet compared to the vegetable and cereal diet in Asia.
source: The early African advantage over Asia may also have been partly due to having a more diverse diet compared to the vegetable and cereal diet in Asia, partly facilitated by lower population density (Deaton, 2007; Moradi, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Rising population, coupled with worsening economic status during structural adjustment, may have undermined earlier dietary advantage in Africa.
source: Rising population, coupled with worsening economic status during structural adjustment, may have undermined earlier dietary advantage (Stevens et al., 2012; Pongou et al., 2006; Weil et al., 1990; Sundberg, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The study used only population-based data that had measured height, which avoids bias in self-reported height.
source: We put particular emphasis on data quality and used only population-based data that had measured height, which avoids bias in self-reported height.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice of the study.

claim: The study used 1472 population-based data sources from all regions of the world.
source: We achieved this by using a large number of population-based data sources from all regions of the world.
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The statistical model could characterize non-linear trends.
source: Finally, we pooled data using a statistical model that could characterize non-linear trends and that used all available data while giving more weight to national data than to subnational and community surveys.
evidence: This describes a feature of the statistical methodology.

claim: The statistical model gave more weight to national data than to subnational and community surveys.
source: Finally, we pooled data using a statistical model that could characterize non-linear trends and that used all available data while giving more weight to national data than to subnational and community surveys.
evidence: This describes a feature of the statistical methodology.

claim: Data in some countries were rather limited or were from community or sub-national studies.
source: Although we have gathered an unprecedentedly comprehensive database of human height and growth, and have applied a statistical model that maximally utilizes the information in these sources, data in some countries were rather limited or were from community or sub-national studies.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of data limitations.

claim: Limited data in some countries is reflected in larger uncertainty of the estimated height in these countries.
source: This is reflected in larger uncertainty of the estimated height in these countries.
evidence: This is a statement about the impact of data limitations on uncertainty.

claim: Greater height in adulthood is beneficially associated with cardiovascular and respiratory diseases.
source: Greater height in adulthood is both beneficially (cardiovascular and respiratory diseases) and harmfully (colorectal, postmenopausal breast and ovarian cancers, and possibly pancreatic, prostate and premenopausal breast cancers) associated with several diseases, independently of its inverse correlation with BMI (Paajanen et al., 2010; Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, 2012; Green et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2015; Batty et al., 2010; World Cancer Research Fund / American Institute for Cancer Research, 2007; 2010; 2011; 2012; 2014a; 2014b; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Greater height in adulthood is harmfully associated with colorectal, postmenopausal breast and ovarian cancers.
source: Greater height in adulthood is both beneficially (cardiovascular and respiratory diseases) and harmfully (colorectal, postmenopausal breast and ovarian cancers, and possibly pancreatic, prostate and premenopausal breast cancers) associated with several diseases, independently of its inverse correlation with BMI (Paajanen et al., 2010; Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, 2012; Green et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2015; Batty et al., 2010; World Cancer Research Fund / American Institute for Cancer Research, 2007; 2010; 2011; 2012; 2014a; 2014b; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Greater height in adulthood is possibly harmfully associated with pancreatic, prostate and premenopausal breast cancers.
source: Greater height in adulthood is both beneficially (cardiovascular and respiratory diseases) and harmfully (colorectal, postmenopausal breast and ovarian cancers, and possibly pancreatic, prostate and premenopausal breast cancers) associated with several diseases, independently of its inverse correlation with BMI (Paajanen et al., 2010; Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, 2012; Green et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2015; Batty et al., 2010; World Cancer Research Fund / American Institute for Cancer Research, 2007; 2010; 2011; 2012; 2014a; 2014b; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research, with a qualifier 'possibly'.

claim: The associations between height and diseases are independent of height's inverse correlation with BMI.
source: Greater height in adulthood is both beneficially (cardiovascular and respiratory diseases) and harmfully (colorectal, postmenopausal breast and ovarian cancers, and possibly pancreatic, prostate and premenopausal breast cancers) associated with several diseases, independently of its inverse correlation with BMI (Paajanen et al., 2010; Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, 2012; Green et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2015; Batty et al., 2010; World Cancer Research Fund / American Institute for Cancer Research, 2007; 2010; 2011; 2012; 2014a; 2014b; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: If the associations in epidemiological studies are causal, the ~20 cm height range in the world is associated with a 17% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality in tall versus short countries.
source: If the associations in epidemiological studies are causal, which is supported by the more recent evidence from Mendelian randomisation studies (Green et al., 2011; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), the ~20 cm height range in the world is associated with a 17% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and 20–40% higher risk of various site-specific cancers, in tall versus short countries.
evidence: This is a conditional claim based on the assumption of causality, supported by Mendelian randomization studies.

claim: If the associations in epidemiological studies are causal, the ~20 cm height range in the world is associated with 20–40% higher risk of various site-specific cancers in tall versus short countries.
source: If the associations in epidemiological studies are causal, which is supported by the more recent evidence from Mendelian randomisation studies (Green et al., 2011; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), the ~20 cm height range in the world is associated with a 17% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and 20–40% higher risk of various site-specific cancers, in tall versus short countries.
evidence: This is a conditional claim based on the assumption of causality, supported by Mendelian randomization studies.

claim: The causal nature of associations between height and diseases is supported by evidence from Mendelian randomisation studies.
source: If the associations in epidemiological studies are causal, which is supported by the more recent evidence from Mendelian randomisation studies (Green et al., 2011; Nüesch et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015), the ~20 cm height range in the world is associated with a 17% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and 20–40% higher risk of various site-specific cancers, in tall versus short countries.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mendelian randomization studies.

claim: Gains in mean population height in successive cohorts are associated with lower mortality in middle and older ages in countries with reliable mortality data (correlation coefficient = −0.58 for men and −0.68 for women).
source: Consistent with individual-level evidence on the association between taller height and lower all-cause mortality in adult ages (Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, 2012), gains in mean population height in successive cohorts are associated with lower mortality in middle and older ages in countries with reliable mortality data (correlation coefficient = −0.58 for men and −0.68 for women) (Figure 11), demonstrating the large impacts of height gain on population health and longevity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, supported by Figure 11 and consistent with prior research.

claim: Short maternal stature increases the risk of small-for-gestational-age and preterm births.
source: Further, short maternal stature increases the risk of small-for-gestational-age and preterm births, both risk factors for neonatal mortality, and of pregnancy complications (Kozuki et al., 2015; Black et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Small-for-gestational-age and preterm births are risk factors for neonatal mortality.
source: Further, short maternal stature increases the risk of small-for-gestational-age and preterm births, both risk factors for neonatal mortality, and of pregnancy complications (Kozuki et al., 2015; Black et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Short maternal stature increases the risk of pregnancy complications.
source: Further, short maternal stature increases the risk of small-for-gestational-age and preterm births, both risk factors for neonatal mortality, and of pregnancy complications (Kozuki et al., 2015; Black et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Improvements vs. stagnation in women's height can influence trends in infant and maternal mortality.
source: Therefore, improvements vs. stagnation in women's height can influence trends in infant and maternal mortality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between maternal height and pregnancy outcomes.

claim: Adult height signifies foetal and early childhood nutrition.
source: Adult height signifies not only foetal and early childhood nutrition, which was included in the Millennium Development Goals, but also that of adolescents (Lancet, 2014).
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding and cited research.

claim: Adult height signifies adolescent nutrition.
source: Adult height signifies not only foetal and early childhood nutrition, which was included in the Millennium Development Goals, but also that of adolescents (Lancet, 2014).
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding and cited research.

claim: Adult height is a link between early-life experiences and NCDs, longevity, education and earnings.
source: Further, adult height is a link between these early-life experiences and NCDs, longevity, education and earnings.
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Height in early adulthood provides a measurable indicator for sustainable development.
source: Therefore, height in early adulthood, which varies substantially across countries and over time, provides a measurable indicator for sustainable development, with links to health and longevity, nutrition, education and economic productivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and the known relationships between height and various outcomes.

claim: The study estimated trends in mean height for adults born from 1896 to 1996 in 200 countries and territories.
source: We estimated trends in mean height for adults born from 1896 to 1996 (i.e., people who had reached their 18th birthday from 1914 to 2014) in 200 countries and territories.
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: The study used data sources that were representative of a national, subnational, or community population and had measured height.
source: We used data sources that were representative of a national, subnational, or community population and had measured height.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for data sources.

claim: The study did not use self-reported height because it is subject to systematic bias.
source: We did not use self-reported height because it is subject to systematic bias that varies by geography, time, age, sex, and socioeconomic characteristics like education and ethnicity (Engstrom et al., 2003; Connor Gorber et al., 2007; Wetmore and Mokdad, 2012; Schenker et al., 2010; Ezzati et al., 2006; Clarke et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citations to research on self-report bias.

claim: The study used data on height in adulthood (18 years of age and older) from 1472 population-based data sources with measurements on over 18.6 million adults born between 1896 and 1996.
source: In this paper, we used data on height in adulthood (18 years of age and older) from the NCD-RisC database for participants born between 1896 and 1996. We used 1472 population-based data sources with measurements on over 18.6 million adults born between 1896 and 1996 whose height had been measured.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: The study had data for 179 of the 200 countries for which estimates were made.
source: We had data for 179 of the 200 countries for which estimates were made; these 179 countries covered 97% of the world's population.
evidence: This describes the data coverage of the study.

claim: The 179 countries with data covered 97% of the world's population.
source: We had data for 179 of the 200 countries for which estimates were made; these 179 countries covered 97% of the world's population.
evidence: This describes the population coverage of the study.

claim: All countries had some data on people born after 1946.
source: All countries had some data on people born after 1946 (second half of analysis period); 134 had data on people born between 1921 and 1945; and 72 had data on people born in 1920 or earlier.
evidence: This describes the temporal distribution of data.

claim: The statistical model had a hierarchical structure in which estimates of mean height for each country and year were nested in regional levels and trends.
source: In summary, the model had a hierarchical structure in which estimates of mean height for each country and year were nested in regional levels and trends, which were in turn nested in those of super-regions and worldwide.
evidence: This describes the structure of the statistical model.

claim: The model estimated change in population mean height over age was linear with a small slope of over 0.2 cm shorter for men and 0.3 cm shorter for women with each decade of older age.
source: In practice, the estimated change in population mean height over age was linear with a small slope of over 0.2 cm shorter for men and 0.3 cm shorter for women with each decade of older age.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical modeling.

claim: 54% of data sources represented national populations.
source: While all our data were from samples of the general population, 796 (54%) of data sources represented national populations, another 199 (14%) major sub-national regions (e.g., one or more provinces or regions of a country), and the remaining 477 (32%) one or a small number of communities.
evidence: This describes the representativeness of the data sources.

claim: 14% of data sources represented major sub-national regions.
source: While all our data were from samples of the general population, 796 (54%) of data sources represented national populations, another 199 (14%) major sub-national regions (e.g., one or more provinces or regions of a country), and the remaining 477 (32%) one or a small number of communities.
evidence: This describes the representativeness of the data sources.

claim: 32% of data sources represented one or a small number of communities.
source: While all our data were from samples of the general population, 796 (54%) of data sources represented national populations, another 199 (14%) major sub-national regions (e.g., one or more provinces or regions of a country), and the remaining 477 (32%) one or a small number of communities.
evidence: This describes the representativeness of the data sources.

claim: The statistical model performed extremely well in validation tests.
source: Our model performed extremely well; specifically, the estimates of mean height were unbiased as evidenced with median errors that were very close to zero globally, and less than ±0.2 cm in every subset of withheld data (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the validation results of the statistical model.

claim: The estimates of mean height were unbiased with median errors very close to zero globally.
source: Our model performed extremely well; specifically, the estimates of mean height were unbiased as evidenced with median errors that were very close to zero globally, and less than ±0.2 cm in every subset of withheld data (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the validation results of the statistical model.

claim: The 95% credible intervals of estimated mean heights covered 97% of true data for both men and women.
source: The 95% credible intervals of estimated mean heights covered 97% of true data for both men and women, which implies good estimation of uncertainty; among subgroups of data, coverage was never < 90%.
evidence: This describes the validation results of the statistical model.

claim: People born in 1896 were shortest in Asia and in Central and Andean Latin America.
source: We estimated that people born in 1896 were shortest in Asia and in Central and Andean Latin America (Figure 1 and Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, supported by Figures 1 and 2.
